title: Right Triangles and Trigonometry
subtitle: Master the Pythagorean theorem, special triangles, SOH-CAH-TOA, and complementary angle identities

sections.title: The Right Triangle Toolkit
sections.content:
Every right triangle question on the SAT uses one or more of these four tools:

1. **Pythagorean theorem:** $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$
2. **SOH-CAH-TOA:** $\sin = \frac{opp}{hyp}$, $\cos = \frac{adj}{hyp}$, $\tan = \frac{opp}{adj}$
3. **Complementary identity:** $\sin\theta = \cos(90° - \theta)$
4. **Special triangles:** 45-45-90 and 30-60-90

Knowing which tool to apply is half the battle.

sections.title: The Pythagorean Theorem and Common Triples
Pythagorean Triples — Memorize These
sections.content:
Instead of computing $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ every time, memorize these right-triangle families:

| Short leg | Long leg | Hypotenuse |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 4 | **5** |
| 5 | 12 | **13** |
| 8 | 15 | **17** |
| 7 | 24 | **25** |

Every **multiple** of these also works: 6-8-10, 9-12-15, 10-24-26, etc.

**How to spot a multiple:** divide all three sides by the same number and check if it's a known triple.

sections.title: Example: Find the Hypotenuse (Triple)
sections.problem: In right triangle $ABC$, the two legs have lengths $24$ and $70$. What is the length of the hypotenuse?

steps.description: Check if 24 and 70 form a multiple of a known triple. Divide both by 2: 12 and 35
12-35-37 is a Pythagorean triple. Scale back up by 2

sections.tip: When you see sides with a common factor, divide them down and check the Pythagorean triple table. This saves you from computing $\sqrt{576 + 4900}$.

sections.title: Special Right Triangles — The SAT's Favorite Shortcuts
45-45-90 Triangle
sections.content:
An **isosceles right triangle** (both legs equal, each angle is 45°, 45°, 90°).

**Side ratios:** if each leg = $s$, then hypotenuse = $s\sqrt{2}$

$$\text{leg} : \text{leg} : \text{hyp} = 1 : 1 : \sqrt{2}$$

**Key relationships:**
- $\text{hypotenuse} = \text{leg} \times \sqrt{2}$
- $\text{leg} = \dfrac{\text{hypotenuse}}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{\text{hyp}\sqrt{2}}{2}$

**When you see it:** a square cut diagonally, or angles of 45°.

sections.title: Example: 45-45-90 Triangle
sections.problem: The diagonal of a square is $10\sqrt{2}$ cm. What is the side length of the square?

steps.description: The diagonal cuts the square into two 45-45-90 triangles. The diagonal is the hypotenuse

sections.tip: Memorize: in a 45-45-90 triangle, the hypotenuse is always the leg times √2. Work backwards: divide by √2 to get the leg.

sections.title: 30-60-90 Triangle
sections.content:
Half of an equilateral triangle. The angles are 30°, 60°, and 90°.

**Side ratios:** if the short leg (opposite 30°) = $s$:

$$\text{short leg} : \text{long leg} : \text{hyp} = 1 : \sqrt{3} : 2$$

| Opposite 30° | Opposite 60° | Hypotenuse |
|---|---|---|
| $s$ | $s\sqrt{3}$ | $2s$ |

**Key relationships:**
- Short leg = hyp ÷ 2
- Long leg = short leg × √3
- **If you know any one side, you can find all three**

sections.title: Example: 30-60-90 Triangle
sections.problem: An equilateral triangle has side length 8. An altitude is drawn from one vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. What is the length of the altitude?

steps.description: The altitude divides the equilateral triangle into two 30-60-90 triangles. The hypotenuse is 8, short leg is 4
The altitude is the long leg (opposite 60°). Long leg = short leg × √3

sections.tip: Any equilateral triangle can be split into two 30-60-90 triangles with an altitude. The altitude is always (side/2)√3.

sections.title: Labeling the Triangle First
sections.content:
'Opposite' and 'adjacent' are **relative to the angle** you're looking at.

For angle $\theta$ in a right triangle:
- **Opposite:** the side across the triangle from $\theta$ (not touching $\theta$)
- **Adjacent:** the leg that touches $\theta$ (not the hypotenuse)
- **Hypotenuse:** always the longest side, always opposite the right angle

**Before writing any trig ratio, label all three sides for the specific angle asked about.**

sections.title: Example: Find a Trig Ratio from Side Lengths
sections.problem: In right triangle $JKL$, $\angle L = 90°$. The legs are $JL = 5$ and $KL = 12$, so the hypotenuse $JK = 13$. What is $\sin J$?

steps.description: Label sides relative to angle J. Opposite to J is KL = 12. Adjacent to J is JL = 5. Hypotenuse = JK = 13

sections.tip: Notice that sin J = 12/13 and cos K = 12/13 as well (since J and K are complementary). Always check: are you being asked about the angle or its complement?

sections.title: Example: Find a Missing Side Using Trig
sections.problem: In right triangle $PQR$, $\angle R = 90°$, $\angle P = 37°$, and $PR = 40$. What is $QR$ (to the nearest integer)?

steps.description: Label sides relative to angle P. QR is opposite P. PR = 40 is adjacent to P

sections.tip: On the SAT, trig ratio questions typically give you exact side lengths — you rarely need to evaluate sin/cos/tan at a specific degree. When you do, use the Desmos scientific calculator.

sections.title: The Complementary Angle Identity — Most Tested Trig Fact
sin and cos Switch for Complementary Angles
sections.content:
In any right triangle, the two acute angles add to $90°$. This gives:

$$\sin(\theta) = \cos(90° - \theta) \qquad \text{and} \qquad \cos(\theta) = \sin(90° - \theta)$$

**In words:** the sine of an angle equals the cosine of its complement.

Example: $\sin(30°) = \cos(60°) = 0.5$

**On the SAT:** If $\angle A + \angle B = 90°$, then $\sin A = \cos B$ and $\cos A = \sin B$. This identity appears on almost every SAT.

sections.title: Example: sin = cos of Complement
sections.problem: In right triangle $RST$, $\angle T = 90°$, so $\angle R + \angle S = 90°$. If $\sin R = \dfrac{\sqrt{15}}{4}$, what is $\cos S$?

steps.description: Since ∠R + ∠S = 90°, angles R and S are complementary

sections.tip: This is a one-step problem. Don't try to compute the angle. Just apply sin(θ) = cos(complement).

sections.title: Example: Solve for an Angle Using Complementary Identity
sections.problem: If $\sin(2x + 10)° = \cos(3x - 20)°$, what is the value of $x$? (Assume all angles are acute.)

steps.description: If sin A = cos B, then A + B = 90°

sections.tip: Key pattern: if sin(expression) = cos(expression), the two expressions must add to 90. Set up the equation and solve.

sections.title: Trig Ratios Depend Only on the Angle, Not the Size
sections.content:
If two right triangles have the same acute angle $\theta$, their trig ratios for that angle are **identical** — regardless of size.

This is because trig ratios are side-to-side ratios, and similar triangles have proportional sides.

**If $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle XYZ$ with $\angle A = \angle X$, then:**
$$\sin A = \sin X, \quad \cos A = \cos X, \quad \tan A = \tan X$$

sections.title: Example: Trig Ratios in Similar Triangles
sections.problem: Triangle $FGH$ is similar to triangle $JKL$ where $\angle F$ corresponds to $\angle J$ and $\angle G$ corresponds to $\angle K$. If $\sin F = \dfrac{308}{317}$, what is $\cos K$?

steps.description: Since triangles are similar, ∠F = ∠J and ∠G = ∠K. The right angle is ∠H = ∠L
Apply complementary identity: sin F = cos of complement of F = cos G = cos K

sections.tip: In this problem, you need BOTH the similar triangles fact AND the complementary identity. First: ∠G = ∠K (corresponding). Second: sin F = cos G (complementary). Therefore cos K = sin F.

sections.title: Example: Build the Full Triangle from One Trig Ratio
sections.problem: In right triangle $XYZ$, $\angle Z = 90°$, $YZ = 24$, and $\tan X = \dfrac{12}{35}$. What is the perimeter of $\triangle XYZ$?

steps.description: tan X = opposite/adjacent. Opposite to X is YZ = 24. Let adjacent XZ = a
Find hypotenuse XY. Note: 24/2 = 12, 70/2 = 35, and 12-35-37 is a triple → hyp = 37 × 2 = 74

sections.tip: tan X = 12/35 tells you the sides are in ratio 12:35. Scale to match the given leg (24 = 12×2), so multiply everything by 2.

sections.title: When to Use Desmos
sections.content:
Desmos is useful for right triangle problems in two scenarios:

**1. Checking your answer:** After solving algebraically, type the equation into Desmos to verify. For example, check that $3^2 + 4^2 = 5^2$ by computing both sides.

**2. Evaluating trig functions:** Use the Desmos scientific calculator (the button at the top left) to compute $\sin$, $\cos$, and $\tan$ values. Make sure Desmos is in degree mode (check the settings).

**3. Finding a missing angle:** If you know sin/cos/tan of an angle, use the inverse functions $\sin^{-1}$, $\cos^{-1}$, $\tan^{-1}$ in the scientific calculator.

**Desmos tip:** For the complementary identity, you can verify: type `sin(30)` and `cos(60)` — both equal 0.5.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: **30-60-90:** sides in ratio 1 : √3 : 2 (short leg : long leg : hyp)
**SOH-CAH-TOA:** label opp/adj/hyp relative to the specific angle FIRST
**Complementary identity:** sin(θ) = cos(90° − θ) — the most-tested trig fact on the SAT
**sin A = cos B** when A + B = 90°; set expressions equal to 90 to solve for unknowns

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Swapping opposite and adjacent (they depend on the angle — label BEFORE applying SOH-CAH-TOA)
- Using diameter instead of radius in Pythagorean calculations involving circles
- 30-60-90: mistaking which leg is opposite 30° vs 60° (short leg is opposite the small angle)
- Forgetting the complementary identity and trying to subtract from 180° instead of 90°
- Setting sin(A) = cos(B) and concluding A = B — instead, A + B = 90

sat_tips: The complementary identity (sin θ = cos(90° - θ)) appears on almost every SAT — know it cold
Memorize the Pythagorean triples to avoid computing square roots: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17
For 30-60-90 triangles: short leg opposite 30°, hyp = 2 × short leg, long leg = short leg × √3
For 45-45-90 triangles: both legs equal; hyp = leg × √2
When sin(expr1) = cos(expr2): set expr1 + expr2 = 90 and solve
